items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: Economists generally expect a large new employer to push up wages in a small town by competing for workers. Examining warehouse openings in forty rural counties, economist Luis Ferreira found that hourly pay at nearby retailers did rise, by about 4 percent in the first year. Many retail workers soon moved to the warehouses, though, and retailers responded by cutting staff and hours rather than raising pay further. Within three years, retail wages had drifted back close to their earlier levels. Taken together, Ferreira's findings suggest that the wage boost from a new large employer may be real but short-lived.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: In the first year after a warehouse opened nearby, hourly pay at local retailers rose by about 4 percent.
Opening a large warehouse is the most effective way for a rural county to raise its long-term wages.
Research suggests that a large new employer may raise local wages at first, but the increase may not last.
Retail wages kept climbing for three years after the warehouses opened, as competition for workers grew.
items.explanation: The middle sentences give separate facts: an early rise, workers leaving retail jobs, and wages falling back. The last sentence adds them up: the boost is 'real but short-lived.' Choice C restates that conclusion and keeps its hedge.

B.why: The passage finds that the wage gain faded, and it never compares warehouses with other ways of raising wages. 'Most effective' and 'long-term' are claims the text does not support.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: The loss of a single predator can reshape an entire ecosystem. Consider Lake Corvin, where heavy angling during the 1990s removed most of the largemouth bass. Freed from their chief predator, small minnows multiplied rapidly. The minnows, in turn, consumed much of the lake's zooplankton, the tiny animals that had kept algae in check. Within a decade, dense algae blooms had clouded the once-clear water, shading out underwater plants that many other species relied on.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Algae bloomed in Lake Corvin after the minnows consumed much of the zooplankton that had grazed on it.

Removing the bass from Lake Corvin had little effect beyond reducing the number of fish anglers caught.
As the case of Lake Corvin shows, losing one predator can set off a chain of changes across an ecosystem.
items.explanation: The first sentence makes a general claim, and the rest of the passage traces one example step by step. Choice D states the claim and connects it to the example the passage uses to support it.

A.why: This accurately describes one link near the end of the chain, but it leaves out the predator and the general point the example is meant to show. You picked a vivid detail instead of the passage's claim.

B.why: The passage describes one lake. It never compares causes of algae blooms or makes a claim about lakes worldwide. You turned a single example into a global ranking.

C.why: The passage says removing the bass led to minnow growth, zooplankton loss, algae blooms, and harm to underwater plants. That is far more than 'little effect'.

items.subtype_name: Main idea of an informational passage
items.stimulus: In the mountain village of Ostrava Alta, residents can hold conversations entirely in whistles. Linguist Tomás Reyna has proposed that this whistled speech arose so that shepherds could talk across steep valleys, and his recordings show that the whistles carry about two kilometers, far beyond the reach of shouted words. Yet, as other researchers point out, showing that the system works well over distance does not show why it began. It may have started as a courtship code or a children's game and only later been put to use across the valleys.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices: Recordings show that the whistled speech of Ostrava Alta carries about two kilometers across the valleys.
The whistles' long range shows that they are useful over distance, but not that this is why they began.
The whistles' long range proves that villagers first developed them to speak across the steep valleys.
Shouted words carry farther than whistles, so the whistled speech most likely began as a children's game.
items.explanation: The passage grants that the whistles carry far, then uses 'Yet' to raise the stronger objection: being useful over distance does not explain how the system began. Choice B keeps both the concession and the limit.

A.why: This is an accurate detail from Reyna's recordings, but it is only the evidence the passage goes on to question. It leaves out the passage's point about the difference between usefulness and origin.

C.why: The first half, about long range, is right. The second half claims 'proves', which is exactly the conclusion the passage says the evidence cannot reach. You recognized the opening and stopped reading.

D.why: The recordings show whistles carry farther than shouted words, not the other way around. The passage also offers the game only as a possibility, not the most likely origin.

items.stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

Kertész's research shows that Varga played no meaningful role in the history of the valley's festivals.
Newly examined records suggest the festival tradition began earlier than credited, under local teachers.
The parish records confirm that Varga organized the valley's first choral festival in the year 1869.
items.explanation: The passage presents the accepted credit to Varga, then 'However' brings in records of an earlier festival led by schoolteachers, backed up by Varga's own letters. Choice C states the correction the whole passage builds toward.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose of a literary excerpt or poem
items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Marisol Okafor's 2014 novel The Load Line. Dessa, a structural engineer, is visiting a pedestrian bridge she designed twenty years earlier.

Dessa had always told her students that a finished bridge belonged to the people who crossed it, not to the person who drew it. She had believed this, or thought she had. Yet standing at midspan now, she caught herself watching each jogger's stride, waiting for the deck to answer with the slight, calculated give she had once spent a winter computing. When a boy stamped his feet to test it, she felt an absurd urge to thank him. The bridge was theirs, she supposed. But some part of it had never stopped being hers.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To convey that Dessa still feels personally attached to a bridge she says belongs to others
To portray a boy's growing curiosity about how the pedestrian bridge he is crossing was built
To describe the specific calculations Dessa carried out in the winter she designed the bridge
To show that Dessa regrets having taught her students an idea she now believes is plainly false
items.explanation: The setup puts Dessa at the center. The passage starts with what she has always believed: a bridge belongs to the people who cross it. Then 'Yet' introduces the correction. She watches the deck closely, wants to thank the boy, and ends by admitting that part of the bridge 'had never stopped being hers.' Taken as a whole, the excerpt shows her lasting personal attachment in spite of what she tells her students.

B.why: You moved the focus from Dessa to the boy. He stamps his feet once, and the passage uses that moment to show Dessa's reaction. It says nothing about his curiosity or about how the bridge was built.

C.why: The text says only that Dessa spent a winter computing the deck's give. It never describes the calculations, so you've picked a detail the text doesn't supply.

D.why: Dessa feels torn, not regretful. She still grants that 'the bridge was theirs.' Nothing suggests she now thinks her teaching was false or wishes she hadn't taught it.

items.subtype_name: Main purpose of a literary excerpt or poem
items.stimulus:
The following text is from Hollis Arden's 2017 poem "To a First-Year Grower." The speaker addresses a new farmer.

You will want the seed to hurry.
Everyone does. The first spring,
you'll kneel each dawn to check the rows
as if watching could pull green from clay.
It can't. But here is what I learned
from forty harvests of beans and doubt:
the waiting is not wasted. Under you,
the roots are doing arithmetic
you cannot see, and by July
the field will show its work.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To warn a new grower that checking the rows too often will damage the young crop
To lament the many seasons the speaker spent doubting whether the beans would grow
To encourage a new grower to trust that growth is happening even when it is unseen
To explain the process by which bean roots draw nutrients out of heavy clay soil
items.explanation: The poem speaks to the new grower. It admits that impatience is natural, and then after 'But' comes the real message: 'the waiting is not wasted,' because the roots are working out of sight and 'by July / the field will show its work.' The tone is reassuring, so the purpose is to encourage the grower to trust growth they can't see yet.

A.why: You turned encouragement into a warning. The speaker says watching can't speed the crop up. The poem never says watching harms it.

B.why: 'Forty harvests of beans and doubt' is the speaker's credential, not a lament. The poem looks ahead with hope, so this choice gets the tone backward.

D.why: 'The roots are doing arithmetic' is a metaphor. The poem never explains how roots take up nutrients, so you've credited it with content it doesn't have.

items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Leland Varga's 2020 novel Fracture Toughness. Imani, a graduate student in materials science, has just watched a ceramic sample she spent months preparing fail a stress test.

The sample broke at less than half the load Imani had predicted, splitting with a sound like a snapped pencil. Dr. Halvorsen was already writing in the lab notebook, murmuring that the fracture pattern was "genuinely interesting." Imani nodded. She knew he meant it kindly, and that he was right: a failure this clean would teach them something. Still, she stood at the press long after he had gone, turning one half over in her gloved hand, unable yet to see it as anything but six months of her life in two pieces.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To show Dr. Halvorsen's excitement about an unexpected result from his laboratory's tests
To portray Imani's lingering disappointment even as she accepts the failure's scientific value
To explain what the fracture pattern revealed about why the ceramic sample broke so early
To suggest that Imani has begun to doubt whether she should remain in materials science
items.explanation: The setup makes Imani the focus. She agrees that the failure 'would teach them something.' The pivot 'Still,' though, shows she can't yet see the broken sample as anything but lost months. The excerpt captures that mix: she accepts the failure's value while still feeling disappointed.

A.why: This is the trap of shifting to the wrong person. Dr. Halvorsen's interest is there to contrast with Imani's feelings. The excerpt is about her reaction, not his.

C.why: The text calls the fracture pattern 'interesting' but never says what it showed. You've picked a finding the passage doesn't report.

D.why: Imani is disappointed about one sample. Nothing in the text says she is questioning her career, so this choice goes well past the evidence.

items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Oona Maris's 2016 short story "The Eyepiece." Teodor is an amateur astronomer.

For thirty years Teodor had assumed that the point of watching the sky was to find something in it: a new comet, a flaring star, some small light that would carry his name. He had found nothing. Yet on the night his granddaughter first looked through his telescope and gasped at Saturn's rings, rings astronomers had cataloged centuries before she was born, he realized he did not mind. The discovery was hers, and it was enough that he had been the one holding the eyepiece steady.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To portray the granddaughter's ambition to someday discover a new object in the night sky
To describe how Teodor's telescope allowed him to observe fine details of Saturn's rings
To suggest that Teodor feels bitter that astronomers cataloged Saturn's rings long ago
To convey Teodor's realization that his granddaughter's delight fulfills him in a new way
items.explanation: The story first states Teodor's long-held assumption that watching the sky is about making a discovery of his own. 'Yet' introduces the correction: watching his granddaughter's delight, he finds he doesn't mind that he never found anything, and helping her is 'enough.' The purpose is to convey that realization.

B.why: The telescope is only the setting. The passage never describes what the rings look like through it, and this choice ignores Teodor's change of heart, which is the point of the excerpt.

C.why: The text says outright that 'he did not mind.' Mentioning that the rings were cataloged long ago stresses that the discovery was hers, not new. It doesn't express any bitterness.

items.stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Faris Adeyemi's 2018 novel Aftershock Season. Lucía is a seismologist monitoring a network of sensors after a moderate earthquake.

The readings came in cleanly, each station reporting on schedule, and for an hour Lucía did what she had trained for years to do: she located the epicenter, estimated the magnitude, and sent the bulletin. Her colleagues praised the speed of it. Only when she walked outside and saw her neighbor sweeping broken dishes from his porch did the numbers on her screen become a morning in someone's kitchen. She set down her coffee and went to help him, the bulletin already feeling strangely small.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To show the pride Lucía's colleagues take in how quickly their team issued the bulletin
To explain the procedure seismologists follow to find an epicenter and estimate magnitude
To portray a moment when Lucía's technical view of the quake gives way to its human impact
To suggest that Lucía believes her monitoring work has no real value to her community
items.explanation: The first sentences show Lucía handling the earthquake as data. The pivot 'Only when' changes that: seeing her neighbor's broken dishes turns 'the numbers on her screen' into something that happened to real people, and she goes to help. The excerpt portrays her shift from a technical view to a human one.

A.why: This is the wrong-person trap. The colleagues' praise gets one sentence, and it sets up the contrast with what Lucía feels afterward. The excerpt is about her.

B.why: The text lists Lucía's tasks but never explains how they're done, and this choice leaves out the turn that the whole excerpt builds toward.

D.why: 'Strangely small' means the bulletin seems minor next to the damage. It doesn't mean she thinks her work is worthless. This choice turns a moment of perspective into a sweeping judgment.

items.stimulus:
The following text is from Ansel Burke's 2021 poem "For the Volunteers Pulling Buckthorn." The speaker addresses people removing an invasive shrub from a forest.

You will not see the oak you're making room for.
Most of you will move away before
the understory fills, before the warblers
find the clearing you made for them.
I know the stems fight back. I know your gloves
tear, and the pile you made looks small
against the hillside's green. Pull anyway.
Some spring you'll never witness,
a trillium will open in the light
your aching hands let in.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices: To encourage the volunteers to keep working even though they may never see the results
To warn the volunteers that invasive plants will likely return to the cleared hillside
To lament that the volunteers will move away before the restored forest can mature
To explain why buckthorn outcompetes native plants such as oak and trillium on hillsides
items.explanation: The speaker addresses the volunteers and admits the hard parts: they won't see the oak, the work is exhausting, and the pile looks small. Then comes the key instruction, 'Pull anyway,' along with the promise that a trillium will bloom because of their effort. The poem is encouraging them to keep going even though someone else will see the results.

B.why: You reversed the tone. The poem never says the buckthorn will come back. It ends with native plants thriving, which is hopeful, not a warning.

C.why: The poem does mention that the volunteers will move away, but only as a reason to 'pull anyway.' Reading it as a lament gets the tone wrong.

D.why: The poem names oak and trillium but never explains how buckthorn competes with them. You've read ecological reasoning into it that isn't there.

The following text is adapted from Greta Lindqvist's 2008 memoir Leaf Beds. The narrator recalls her first fossil-collecting trip with her father, a paleobotanist.

The following text is adapted from Idris Calloway's 2019 novel The Surveyor's Daughter. In the 1880s, Nell is helping her father complete a map of a river valley.

D.why: The passage does treat the fossil as a treasure, so this fits the mood. But the word describes what the veins look like, and "valuable as thread" doesn't make sense.

items.stimulus:
The following text is from a story about an immunologist.

Dr. Okafor leaned back from the microscope and rubbed her eyes. The body, she thought, kept a longer memory than most people did. A virus met once in childhood, and survived, would be recognized decades later, and the defending cells would gather so quickly that the invader was routed before its host even felt the first ache of illness.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word "routed" most nearly mean?
items.explanation: The defending cells gather quickly and the invader is dealt with before any illness appears. That is a victory, so "routed" means defeated.

items.subtype_name: Use the vertex and symmetry of a parabola
items.stimulus: A sports scientist filming a volleyball serve modeled the ball's height above the floor with the function $h(t) = -5t^2 + 13t + 1.5$, where $h(t)$ is the height, in meters, $t$ seconds after the serve. The model shows the ball at a height of 5.9 meters when $t = 0.4$.
items.stem: At what other time $t$, in seconds, is the ball's height 5.9 meters?
items.explanation: The vertex is at $t = -\frac{b}{2a} = -\frac{13}{2(-5)} = 1.3$. A parabola is symmetric about its vertex, so a height reached 0.9 seconds before the peak is reached again 0.9 seconds after it: $2(1.3) - 0.4 = 2.2$. Check: $h(2.2) = -24.2 + 28.6 + 1.5 = 5.9$.

A.why: 1.3 seconds is when the ball reaches its highest point, which is the vertex. You found the axis of symmetry but didn't use it to find the matching time on the far side of the peak.

B.why: You added 0.4 to the vertex time. The matching time is the same distance past the vertex as 0.4 is before it, so you need $1.3 + (1.3 - 0.4)$, not $1.3 + 0.4$.

D.why: You doubled the vertex time and forgot to subtract 0.4. 2.6 seconds is actually when the ball comes back down to its starting height of 1.5 meters, not to 5.9 meters.

items.subtype_name: Use the vertex and symmetry of a parabola
items.stimulus: A musicologist studying recordings of a symphony models how the conductor's tempo drifts from the marked tempo. The function $d(x) = ax^2 + bx + c$, where $a$, $b$, and $c$ are constants, gives the deviation from the marked tempo, in beats per minute, $x$ minutes into the movement. In the xy-plane, the graph of $y = d(x)$ has its vertex at $(4, -6)$ and crosses the x-axis at two points.
items.stem: Which of the following could be the value of $c$?
items.explanation: In vertex form, $d(x) = a(x - 4)^2 - 6$. The vertex is below the x-axis, so the graph can only cross the axis twice if it opens upward, which means $a > 0$. Expanding gives $c = 16a - 6$, and with $a > 0$ that means $c > -6$. Only 10 works, with $a = 1$: $(x - 4)^2 - 6$ has two real roots.

A.why: This value comes from $a = -1$. A parabola that opens downward from a vertex at $y = -6$ never reaches the x-axis, so it can't have two x-intercepts.

B.why: You used a vertex of $(4, 6)$. With that vertex, a downward-opening parabola would cross twice, and $a = -\frac{1}{4}$ gives $c = -10$. With the actual vertex $(4, -6)$, though, $a = -\frac{1}{4}$ opens downward and never crosses the axis.

C.why: $-6$ is the y-coordinate of the vertex, not the y-intercept. $c = -6$ would also need $a = 0$, and then the function wouldn't be quadratic at all.

D.why: 28 is the value of $4x$, not $x$. You stopped one step early and didn't divide by 4.

items.subtype_name: Support a contrast, cause or prediction with two parts
items.stimulus: Surviving linen bolts from two neighboring fifteenth-century Flemish towns differ in a telling way. Thread counts in bolts from Hoverzele vary little from one bolt to the next, while bolts from Mantegem are far less uniform, even though weavers in both towns used similar looms and local flax. items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Maes's conclusion?
choices: Weavers in both Hoverzele and Mantegem were paid by the finished bolt, and output in the two towns rose at about the same rate after 1432.
Hoverzele bolts woven before 1432 vary in thread count about as much as Mantegem bolts do, while Hoverzele bolts woven afterward are far more uniform.
Across all of the surviving bolts, those from Hoverzele show much more uniform thread counts than those from Mantegem, by a wide and consistent margin.
Mantegem also required each bolt to be inspected before sale, but its inspectors measured only a bolt's length and never its thread count.
items.explanation: Maes names a specific cause, the 1432 inspection rule, for a specific result, Hoverzele's uniform cloth. If Hoverzele cloth was as uneven as Mantegem's until 1432 and became uniform only after it, the change lines up with the rule, which separates the rule from other differences between the towns. This choice ties the cause to the effect.

items.stimulus: In 2019 the city of Harlow Bay added curb-protected bike lanes to twelve arterial streets, narrowing each street's car lanes from 3.6 to 3.0 meters; twelve similar arterials were left unchanged. items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Quist's claim?
choices: Average driving speeds fell by similar amounts on the redesigned arterials and on the unchanged arterials during the three years after 2019.
Reported car crashes on the redesigned arterials were about 30 percent lower in the three years after 2019 than in the three years before.

The number of cyclists using the redesigned arterials tripled after 2019, while cyclist numbers on the unchanged arterials stayed roughly the same.

items.subtype_name: Support a contrast, cause or prediction with two parts
items.stimulus: Astronomer Ines Carvalho's team used a space telescope to survey 40 rocky planets orbiting red dwarf stars. Planets around slowly rotating stars were far more likely to show signs of an atmosphere than planets around rapidly rotating ones. items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the team's conclusion?

Around both kinds of star, planets on wider orbits were likelier to show atmospheres than planets on closer orbits, and by similar margins.
The rapidly rotating stars in the sample flared less often than the slowly rotating stars did, although their individual flares were brighter.
items.explanation: The team says flares, not rotation, are the cause. To support that, a finding has to pull the two apart. Fast rotators that rarely flare have planets with atmospheres at the slow-rotator rate, so when flares are absent, fast rotation alone doesn't cost planets their atmospheres. That points to flares.

At a dozen other sites nearby, Osmunda spores reappear above the boundary wherever the ash is thin and are absent wherever it is thick.

Brun engraved chiefly on end-grain boxwood, and Collet turned to pearwood only for its largest and cheapest commissions.

items.stimulus: Male song sparrows in city parks sing with a higher minimum pitch than woodland males do, which helps their songs carry over low-frequency traffic noise. Males that had heard urban tutors sang higher than the other males only while recordings of traffic noise were being played to them.

items.subtype_name: Support a contrast, cause or prediction with two parts
items.stimulus: Japanese barberry, an invasive shrub, has spread through many forests in the northeastern United States. Ecologist Nadia Ferrante observed that it spreads fastest in forests with dense populations of white-tailed deer. Deer rarely browse barberry's spiny stems but readily eat the seedlings of native shrubs such as spicebush. Ferrante therefore hypothesizes that deer aid barberry indirectly: by eating native seedlings, they remove competitors that would otherwise shade out young barberry plants.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Ferrante's hypothesis?

Across the region, barberry covered more of the forest floor in forests with many deer than in forests with few or no deer at all.
Deer eat some barberry berries, and seeds that pass through a deer's gut sprout readily, letting deer carry barberry to new sites.
In fenced and unfenced plots alike, spicebush seedlings that survived their first year began flowering at about the same age.
items.explanation: Ferrante's claim runs from deer, to fewer native seedlings, to faster barberry spread. The fenced and unfenced plots differ in one thing, access by deer, and this choice shows both the middle step (native seedlings eaten) and the end result (barberry spreading) changing with it.

B.why: You picked a restatement of Ferrante's starting observation. It links deer to barberry but shows nothing about the middle step, the loss of native competitors.

C.why: You picked a different way deer could help barberry. Spreading seeds would account for the result, but it isn't the competition mechanism Ferrante proposes, so it doesn't support her hypothesis.

D.why: You picked a detail that is the same in both groups. Flowering age among seedlings that survived doesn't separate the fenced and unfenced plots or say anything about how barberry spreads.
